_comment:
Conformance vectors for the policy decision — the condition grammar and the walk — written as data so a reimplementation in another language is answerable to the same cases. They come from rail-center's docs/policy-evaluation-contract.md, under `Conditions` and `The decision`. This repository is where they live; rail-center's api/tests/vectors/policy_evaluation.json covers the same contract from the publishing side.

What is NOT here. Whether a bundle can be READ at all: that refusal is eager, taken before the walk, and tests/vectors/bundle.json carries it. How an MCP message resolves to an endpoint key: that is this gateway's own composition, it appears nowhere in the contract, and tests/test_endpoint.py covers it. What a decision means for a call naming NO endpoint: the contract models endpoint_key as an argument that is always present, so it takes no position on one, and every case here carries a key. tests/test_decide.py carries this gateway's own answer. How the `x-rail` header decodes: tests/vectors/ticket.json.

Every case carries `endpoint_key` — the RESOLVED key, never a raw ingress path — and `now`, a fixed instant, because a decision is a pure function of its inputs and a pure function is the only thing two implementations can be compared on. The ticket comes as either `claims`, which the runner base64url-encodes, or `header`, a literal the runner passes through unchanged. `agent_id` and `exp` are spelled out on every payload rather than filled in by a runner, so a case can be read literally.

Cases come in two shapes.

A CONDITION case carries `condition` and `holds`. The runner puts the condition behind a single enabled `block` policy at priority 1, walks it, and reads `holds` off the decision: a condition that holds denies, and one that does not allows. Going through the decision rather than calling a predicate directly is what makes these vectors rather than unit tests of a private function.

A BUNDLE case carries a whole `bundle` and an `expect` of `allowed`, `denied_by` (a canonical policy id, or null) and `alerts` (canonical policy ids, IN EVALUATION ORDER — priority ascending, ties by canonical id — not in the order the bundle listed them).

A case of either shape may carry `refusal` instead, naming the kind of refusal required: `uninterpretable_condition`. Read it and assert on it. A runner that asks only 'did it throw?' scores a crash as conformant, and a crash is the one outcome the contract rules out everywhere — an exception where a decision belongs is neither an allow nor a deny.

`ticket_state`, where a case carries it, is what the header must classify as; its absence means the case does not assert one. `note` says why a case exists where its name does not.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a field outside the table
cases.note: Rail Center can learn a field this enforcement point has not. The natural shape — a lookup defaulting to false — silently stops enforcing a block rule.

cases.name: uninterpretable — an operator outside the table
uninterpretable — skill_match does not admit eq
uninterpretable — endpoint_key does not admit missing
cases.note: It is an argument to the decision rather than a claim that may be absent, so `missing` could never hold.

cases.name: uninterpretable — endpoint_key does not admit present
cases.note: The other half: `present` would always hold.

cases.name: uninterpretable — skills does not admit eq
uninterpretable — skills does not admit in
uninterpretable — only endpoint_key admits matches
cases.note: A pattern over an attacker-chosen claim is a subtler control than it looks.

cases.name: uninterpretable — agent_id does not admit contains
uninterpretable — posture_score does not admit matches
uninterpretable — a string operand for an ordered operator
cases.note: Not a rule that is false — one that can never be true, which is the failure an operator is least likely to notice.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a list operand for an ordered operator
uninterpretable — a boolean operand for an ordered operator
cases.note: A boolean is not a number, here or in the reference.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a null operand for an ordered operator
uninterpretable — a non-scalar operand for eq
uninterpretable — a boolean operand for ne
uninterpretable — a null operand for eq
uninterpretable — a non-list operand for in
uninterpretable — a non-scalar operand for contains
uninterpretable — a non-string pattern for matches
cases.note: Refused at validation rather than treated as a pattern that never matches: the key is always a string, so a non-string pattern can never hold.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a condition that is not an object
uninterpretable — a condition that is a list
uninterpretable — a field that is not a string
uninterpretable — an operator that is not a string
uninterpretable — a field that is missing entirely
uninterpretable — an operator that is missing entirely
uninterpretable — an unknown field is refused even where no ticket was read
cases.note: The refusal is a property of the rule, not of what it would have resolved against. A reader that resolved first and refused second would answer differently here.

cases.name: x_rail_header is missing for an absent ticket
cases.note: no header at all. All four unusable states fold into one answer, which is what makes the seeded P0 a rule about trustworthy identity rather than about whether a header was physically transmitted.

cases.name: x_rail_header is missing for an undecodable ticket
cases.note: a header that does not decode. All four unusable states fold into one answer, which is what makes the seeded P0 a rule about trustworthy identity rather than about whether a header was physically transmitted.

cases.name: x_rail_header is missing for an expired ticket
x_rail_header is missing for a malformed ticket
cases.note: No string agent_id, so the payload is readable and is not a ticket.

cases.name: x_rail_header is present for a valid ticket
x_rail_header is not missing for a valid ticket
an expired ticket's posture_score does not outlive it
cases.note: The claims are still readable as text and are not a basis for any decision. This is the case that rule exists for.

cases.name: an expired ticket's claims are absent rather than retained
a claim whose key is absent from the payload resolves to absent
cases.note: The one an implementation forgets: reading claims[field] and testing === null leaves an omitted key reading as present. Deleting a key from an unsigned ticket is free.

cases.name: a claim that is present and null resolves to absent
cases.note: posture_score is null for an agent registered but not yet scored, and the seeded rule meaning 'deny an unscored agent' has to catch it.

cases.name: a claim that is present and null is not present
a claim of zero is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of zero is not missing
a claim of an empty string is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of an empty string is not missing
a claim of an empty list is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of an empty list is not missing
skill_match is present when skills lists the endpoint key
skill_match is missing when skills lists something else
skill_match is missing when the ticket declares no skills
a string skills is not a one-element list of itself
cases.note: It declares no skill at all — the same reading `contains` takes.

cases.name: an object skills declares no skill either
cases.note: The guard is on the claim being a list. A reader guarding only against null iterates this object's keys and finds the endpoint key among them, so a forged ticket declares a skill it does not carry.

cases.name: a numeric skills declares no skill
skill_match is missing where a matching skill sits inside a nested list
cases.note: Membership is compared element by element, and a list is not the key.

cases.name: skill_match is missing when no usable ticket was read
endpoint_key resolves to the key the decision was given
agent_id — present holds on the claim
cases.note: The table carries eleven fields, and this group pins the five that are read straight off the claims. A field the table stops carrying is not a condition that fails to hold: it refuses the request, so a rule Rail Center published against it answers 503 here on every request whose walk reaches it and decides normally there.

cases.name: agent_id — missing holds where no usable ticket was read
cases.note: A ticket is not valid without a string agent_id, so this claim is absent only where the ticket itself is unusable — which is the one way the field can answer missing at all.

cases.name: agent_id — eq holds against the claim
agent_id — ne holds against a different value
agent_id — in holds for a member
sandbox_id — present holds on the claim
sandbox_id — missing holds where the payload omits the key
cases.note: Reading a ticket turns on agent_id and exp alone, so a payload without this claim is a valid ticket carrying an absent claim rather than an unreadable one. The ticket is unsigned: deleting a key is free, and a rule keying on this field has to survive it.

cases.name: sandbox_id — eq holds against the claim
sandbox_id — ne holds against a different value
sandbox_id — in holds for a member
sandbox_type — present holds on the claim
sandbox_type — missing holds where the payload omits the key
sandbox_type — eq holds against the claim
sandbox_type — ne holds against a different value
sandbox_type — in holds for a member
environment_fingerprint — present holds on the claim
environment_fingerprint — missing holds where the payload omits the key
environment_fingerprint — eq holds against the claim
environment_fingerprint — ne holds against a different value
environment_fingerprint — in holds for a member
scored_at — present holds on the claim
scored_at — missing holds until scoring has run
cases.note: Null until posture is computed, by the same rule that leaves posture_score null, and absent by the same door as a key that is not there.

cases.name: scored_at — eq holds against the claim
scored_at — ne holds against a different value
scored_at — in holds for a member
eq compares a string to a string
a string never equals a number
cases.note: "40" does not satisfy eq 40. JavaScript's == and Number() both coerce and must not be used.

cases.name: an empty string never equals zero
a boolean claim never equals one
cases.note: True == 1 in Python and true === 1 is false in TypeScript, so a reader that does not exclude booleans makes a rule's meaning depend on which language read it.

cases.name: a boolean claim never equals zero
a non-scalar claim does not satisfy eq
a string posture_score is catchable by eq against the same string
cases.note: An allow-list of forgeries rather than a type check, and the difference between 'hard to express' and 'not expressible'.

cases.name: and does not hold against a numeric claim of the same value
ne holds for a different scalar
ne does not hold for an absent field
cases.note: A rule meaning 'absent or different' is two conditions.

cases.name: a boolean claim does not satisfy ne
cases.note: Not comparing is not the same as comparing unequal.

cases.name: a list claim does not satisfy ne
cases.note: Reachable through a forged claim, and the case that catches a reader that negates without checking the kinds first.

cases.name: an object claim does not satisfy ne
lt compares two numbers
a numeric string does not satisfy lt
cases.note: It is not a number at all. The ordered operators must check the type before comparing rather than convert.

cases.name: a boolean claim does not satisfy lt
a list claim does not satisfy lt
lte holds at the bound
lt does not hold at the bound
gte holds at the bound
gt holds above it
a float claim compares against a whole operand
two integers a double cannot separate are equal
cases.note: 2**53 and 2**53 + 1 are distinct integers in an arbitrary-precision language and the same double in JavaScript. Every number reaching a comparison is narrowed, on both sides of it.

cases.name: and neither is less than the other
cases.note: The other half. Narrowing only the claim leaves the divergence on the operand.

cases.name: an integer past the double range saturates rather than raising
cases.note: Both saturate to the same infinity and compare equal. float() raises where JavaScript saturates, and an exception where a comparison belongs is neither an allow nor a deny.

cases.name: and so does one past the negative end
an operand overflowing to infinity is compared, not refused
in holds for a member
in does not coerce its elements
in holds for a numeric member
a non-scalar claim is a member of nothing
a non-scalar element of an in operand never matches
cases.note: Accepted by validation and simply never matches, so no comparison ever sees two containers.

cases.name: a boolean element of an in operand never matches a boolean claim
contains holds when the list carries the operand
contains does not substring-match a string claim
cases.note: A reader reaching for `operand in claim` would satisfy a rule about delivery.admin with a skills of delivery.administrator.

cases.name: contains does not substring-match an element either
contains requires the claim to be a list
a boolean element of a list claim does not satisfy contains
matches — a trailing star covers a whole segment
matches — a star spans the segment separator
cases.note: `*` includes the `.` that separates endpoint-key segments.

cases.name: matches — a star stands for an empty run
matches — a pattern is anchored at the start
cases.note: A pattern matching anywhere within the key would be a different rule from the one an operator reads it as.

cases.name: matches — a leading star covers everything before the suffix
matches — a pattern is anchored at the end
matches — a bare star matches any key
matches — a pattern carrying no star is a literal
cases.note: It matches exactly what `eq` would. Accepted rather than refused, because refusing it would mean broadening a rule from `delivery.orders` to `delivery.*` had to change the operator too.

cases.name: matches — a literal is not a prefix rule
cases.note: A reader answering `key.startswith(pattern)` on the starless branch widens every literal pattern an operator wrote.

cases.name: matches — a literal does not match a longer key
matches — the two ends may abut
cases.note: Pinned from both sides, because startswith-and-endswith is the natural shape to write.

cases.name: matches — the two ends must not overlap
cases.note: `ab*ab` does not match `ab`, though the key both starts and ends with `ab`. `*` stands for a run of characters, possibly empty, but never for characters counted twice.

cases.name: matches — the two ends with a run between them
matches — a key too short for both ends
matches — an interior segment must fit before the suffix
cases.note: A reader that checks only that the segment was found lets it match the suffix's own characters a second time.

cases.name: matches — and does fit where the key carries it twice
matches — an interior segment matched at its earliest position
cases.note: With `*` the only metacharacter every interior segment is a fixed literal, so taking one early never rules out a match a fuller search would find — which is why no backtracking is needed to be correct.

cases.name: matches — two stars are one
matches — two stars are one, over a run
matches — an embedded newline is an ordinary character in a pattern
matches — a star matches a newline
cases.note: `.` does not without re.DOTALL in Python or the `s` flag in JavaScript, so the default regex translation of `*` to `.*` refuses a key this accepts.

cases.name: matches — a literal does not match a key with a trailing newline
cases.note: Python's `$` matches immediately before a trailing newline, so a `^…$` translation accepts a key this rule does not name. The two newline rules pull in opposite directions and a translation can get either wrong alone.

cases.name: matches — no case folding, on the key
cases.note: `FinRetail.*` matches nothing that `finretail.*` matches. Folding would reintroduce the divergence in the form nobody writes a test for, because the locale-sensitive way to fold sits a keystroke from the locale-independent one.

cases.name: matches — no case folding, on the pattern
matches — no Unicode normalisation
cases.note: `é` and `e` plus a combining acute (`́`) are canonically equivalent and are not the same key here. Normalising both sides to NFC is a habit picked up from path handling, and it makes the set of keys a rule covers depend on which form the operator's editor saved.

cases.name: matches — the same form matches itself
cases.note: So the case above is a statement about normalisation rather than about the pattern being wrong.

cases.name: matches — a question mark is a literal
cases.note: Every character but `*` is a literal — `?`, `[`, `]` and `\` included — and there is no escape character.

cases.name: matches — a question mark matches itself
matches — a bracket expression is not a character class
cases.note: Python's fnmatch supports `[seq]` and `[!seq]` and folds case on some platforms, which is why it must not be used.

cases.name: matches — a bracket expression matches itself
matches — a backslash is a literal
matches — a backslash does not escape a star
cases.note: There being no escape character means a literal `*` cannot be written; an endpoint key containing one is matched by `eq`.

cases.name: an endpoint with no binding entry is subject to every policy
cases.note: Read the other way round it is a total loss of enforcement, which is why the contract states it twice.

cases.name: a binding narrows to the policies it names
cases.note: The low-score rule matches and is not in this endpoint's chain.

cases.name: a binding in mode open narrows to nothing and the walk allows
cases.note: **Do not fall back to the whole chain when narrowing empties it.** Rail Center has a fallback of exactly that shape and it belongs to the publishing side alone: it drops a binding whose policies are all absent or disabled before the bundle is written. Copying it here makes the two sides disagree — deny there, allow here.

cases.name: a binding naming only a disabled policy narrows to nothing too
cases.note: The same empty narrowing by the other route, and the one a publishing-side fallback would turn into a denial by the whole chain.

cases.name: a bound id spelled non-canonically still narrows
cases.note: Both sides of the membership test are canonicalised, so a non-canonically spelled id matches its policy rather than nothing.

cases.name: the first matching denying policy wins and stops the walk
cases.note: A lower priority number is genuinely higher precedence rather than merely earlier in a list that keeps being read.

cases.name: priority 9 precedes priority 10
cases.note: Numerically, not as text: a default string comparator gets this backwards.

cases.name: equal priorities are separated by the canonical id
cases.note: An implementation reading two equal priorities must not be free to choose, or the two sides disagree exactly where the policies conflict.

cases.name: a non-canonically spelled id is reported canonically
cases.note: A decision reporting the bundle's own spelling names the same policy two ways across a decision and its denial report.

cases.name: the denial names the policy that actually matched
cases.note: An implementation reporting the first rule in its chain produces a record that is wrong and that nothing downstream will contradict.

cases.name: alerts that accumulated before a denial travel with it
cases.note: An alert that matched on a request a later denial stopped is still something an operator asked to be told about.

cases.name: alerts accumulate in evaluation order, not in the order the bundle listed them
cases.note: Listed at priorities [2, 3, 1] precisely so a reader that accumulates in bundle order fails it.

cases.name: an alert never denies
any action that is not alert denies — an action this build cannot read
cases.note: The database constrains action to block or alert; an enforcement point builds policies from wire JSON where no such constraint reaches. A matched policy whose action cannot be read is still a matched policy.

cases.name: any action that is not alert denies — the right action in the wrong case
cases.note: The database constrains action to block or alert; an enforcement point builds policies from wire JSON where no such constraint reaches. A matched policy whose action cannot be read is still a matched policy.

cases.name: any action that is not alert denies — a near miss for `alert`
cases.note: The database constrains action to block or alert; an enforcement point builds policies from wire JSON where no such constraint reaches. A matched policy whose action cannot be read is still a matched policy.

cases.name: any action that is not alert denies — no action at all
cases.note: The database constrains action to block or alert; an enforcement point builds policies from wire JSON where no such constraint reaches. A matched policy whose action cannot be read is still a matched policy.

cases.name: any action that is not alert denies — an action that is not a string
cases.note: The database constrains action to block or alert; an enforcement point builds policies from wire JSON where no such constraint reaches. A matched policy whose action cannot be read is still a matched policy.

cases.name: a policy that matches nothing denies nothing
an empty chain allows
a chain of only disabled policies allows
cases.note: A disabled policy is skipped, not evaluated and discarded.

cases.name: a policy missing the enabled key is enabled
cases.note: A rule an operator never switched off is one they expect to be running.

cases.name: enabled must be exactly false to skip
cases.note: Not merely falsy: `[]` is falsy in Python and truthy in JavaScript.

cases.name: a disabled policy's condition is never read
cases.note: The remedy for a rule nobody can read is to switch it off, and that only works if disabling is decided before interpreting.

cases.name: a rule the walk never reaches changes nothing
cases.note: **The refusal is lazy.** The walk stops at the first match, so a rule at priority 9 is never reached once priority 1 has denied, and that request has a clean answer. Refusing the whole bundle up front turns one bad condition into a total outage and answers differently here.

cases.name: a rule the walk does reach refuses the request, alerts and all
cases.note: What separates 'refuse the request' from 'refuse but keep the alerts' and from 'skip the rule and keep walking'. Alerts already accumulated are discarded with the decision: they were the first half of a verdict that was never reached.

cases.name: a rule behind an unreadable one is never consulted
cases.note: The refusal comes first in the chain, so the walk ends there whatever the later rule would have answered.

cases.name: the seeded chain denies a request carrying no ticket
the seeded chain denies a low-scoring agent by the rule for it
the seeded chain allows a scored agent presenting a valid ticket
an unscored agent is denied by a rule about an absent score
cases.note: posture_score is null until scoring runs. A reader that lets a null read as present stops this rule firing on exactly the agents it exists for — and `lt 40` would not catch them either, since an ordered operator does not hold against an absence.

cases.name: an unscored agent is not caught by the low-score rule
cases.note: The other half of the pair above, and why the seeded chain needs both rules rather than one.
